text: I am checking whether P’s room-conditioned door search is a genuine learning-augmented decision problem. Initial concern: Q’s guarantees are for an explicit online objective and comparator, while P reports detection geometry and topology without a prediction-independent door-search baseline. I will inspect P’s gating and revision mechanisms for a sharper, architecture-specific result.

The abstract-scan connection is valid but underspecified. Q, \S Background (lines 257-343), requires a declared prediction, task loss, benchmark, and consistency/robustness/smoothness criterion; its cascade proposition (lines 1069-1110) says component bounds do not compose without downstream benchmark distortion and an error-sensitive edge. P, Door-Concept Agent (lines 352-389), uses estimated room walls \(\hat W\) in a hard \(\delta=0.15\mathrm{m}\) point filter before door-edge extraction, while P, Detection Mistakes (lines 613-633), says validated wrong rooms remain fixed and can lack revision. A promising pair-specific question is whether this hard gate makes door recall discontinuous in room-wall error, and what fallback/revision assumptions permit a bound on missed doors and exploration cost.

P-specific bottleneck: the door agent is dormant until a current room exists (P.tex lines 230, 416), then Algorithm 2 hard-filters LiDAR points by \(\operatorname{dist}(p,\widehat W)\leq\delta\) with \(\delta=0.15\,\mathrm m\), before edge pairing and a wall-membership test (P.tex lines 354-385). If an accepted room omits a real wall, no downstream prediction-matching can recover its door because the relevant evidence never enters the candidate set. P explicitly reports fixed accepted concepts and missing revision (lines 615-630). Q warns that local triples do not compose without interface sensitivity/benchmark control (Q.tex lines 1023-1026, 1097-1109); its error-propagation proposition assumes a Lipschitz edge, which this hard gate may violate at threshold. This suggests studying candidate retention and search cost under bounded room error, with a prediction-independent fallback.

Candidate theorem/design, sharper than abstract LAA mapping. Let \(W^*\) be true wall set, \(\widehat W\) the accepted room walls, and \(S^*\) true door endpoint points. If \(\sup_{w\in W^*}\operatorname{dist}(w,\widehat W)\leq\epsilon\) and \(\sup_{p\in S^*}\operatorname{dist}(p,W^*)\leq b\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(p,\widehat W)\leq b+\epsilon\). Thus widening P’s first gate to \(\delta\geq b+\epsilon\) guarantees these endpoints survive. This alone does NOT guarantee door recall: P’s later exact wall-membership/width tests and its derivative-based peak extraction can still reject them; a theorem must make those stages tolerant or explicitly assume candidate completeness. Without a finite bound on omitted walls, scenes identical inside the retained strip but differing by a door on an omitted wall are indistinguishable to this gated detector, so no prediction-independent recall guarantee is possible without fallback/revision. A viable result would couple certified recall to the expanded strip’s \(\binom{n(\epsilon)}2\) pair cost and invoke a full-scan fallback when the room certificate fails.

A precise obstruction: define discovery latency as scans until an actually visible door is reported, and compare to a prediction-free full-field detector that reports it in finite scans. P\(\text{\u2019}\)s room-conditioned detector never processes points farther than \(\delta=0.15\mathrm{m}\) from \(\hat W\) (Algorithm 2, lines 352-390), and its door agent activates only after a current room node (lines 195-205, 391ff). In an environment where a validated but wrong room model places a true door\(\text{\u2019}\)s evidence outside that band on every visit, and the room is never revised as P explicitly states (lines 613-633), discovery latency is infinite while the full-field comparator can be finite. Thus no finite prediction-independent competitive ratio for that discovery objective follows from P\(\text{\u2019}\)s current architecture. This is conditional on a persistent wrong wall, a visible door, and a complete enough full-field baseline; it is not a claim about P\(\text{\u2019}\)s reported simulator runs.

Alternative checked: P’s LTSM predicts/loads known destination rooms near doors and unloads remote rooms (P.tex lines 429-456); Q has a fully specified learning-augmented caching/paging framework (Q.tex lines 806-834). This is a cleaner formal match than door detection, but P’s current implementation mainly keeps the current room and anticipates its neighbor, so a new paging theorem would need a multi-room memory budget, load latency/energy, and a request sequence induced by navigation. The pair alone supplies no such performance evidence. I currently prefer the P-specific door-gate question, where an explicit information-loss obstruction and margin certificate can be proved using the actual algorithm.

External prior-work check: query `site:arxiv.org "learning-augmented" "search" predictions robust exploration` found Eberle et al., Robustification of Online Graph Exploration Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05422 . It already proves error-sensitive robustification for online graph exploration, so a generic claim that LAA plus robotic exploration is new would be false. The potentially specific gap here is upstream semantic censoring: P\(\text{\u2019}\)s estimated walls determine which raw points reach the detector and which door hypotheses/active visits can even be proposed. A matching residual computed only on retained evidence cannot by itself certify excluded regions. Need state any new result as a candidate-retention/coverage guarantee for this architecture, with explicit sensor and comparator assumptions, and test against existing exploration robustifiers.

Prior-work check (queries: `site:arxiv.org learning augmented algorithms geometric search uncertain predicted region fallback recall object detection`; `site:arxiv.org robust object detection predicted region of interest missed objects fallback search guarantee`; `site:arxiv.org "learning-augmented" "exploration" "prediction"`) found Eberle et al., Robustification of Online Graph Exploration Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05422, which already gives prediction-sensitive robustification for graph exploration. It does not, from its abstract, address P’s upstream hard geometric gate. Search also found Xu et al., Deep Interactive Object Selection, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.00243, whose introduction notes predicted rectangles as hard constraints can omit object/context; this is analogous censoring, so the general failure pattern is not novel. I claim only a prospective P-specific, formally and empirically tested result, not novelty established by this search.

Sharpened research question: for P\(\text{\u2019}\)s room-wall-conditioned door search, can a wall-error certificate plus occasional prediction-independent audits guarantee both retention of real door evidence and bounded search cost, while exploiting the narrow wall strip when the room model is right? Elementary lemma: for any relevant LiDAR point \(p\), if \(\operatorname{dist}(p,W^*)\leq b\) and one-sided wall error \(\sup_{w\in W^*}\operatorname{dist}(w,\hat W)\leq\epsilon\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(p,\hat W)\leq b+\epsilon\). Thus a widened gate at \(\delta\geq b+\epsilon\) retains those points. The hard threshold otherwise admits a jump in retained candidates from an arbitrarily small wall perturbation for points whose gate margin approaches zero, so Q\(\text{\u2019}\)s Lipschitz composition condition (Q lines 1097-1110) is unavailable without a margin/tolerant formulation. This lemma stops before P\(\text{\u2019}\)s derivative threshold and exact-looking wall/width checks; those need separate margins or a different candidate generator.

Correction to #8: arXiv:1707.00243 is titled Deep GrabCut for Object Selection, not Deep Interactive Object Selection. Its abstract explicitly says rectangle priors may be too large or too small and uses a soft distance-map constraint (https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00243). It supplies an analogy for hard-region censoring, not a door-detection theorem. Eberle et al. abstract confirms learning-augmented graph exploration robustification (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05422), but that is after the graph is available and does not establish completeness of door discovery.

Do not oversell the positive lemma as a door-detection theorem or a publication by itself. P\(\text{\u2019}\)s Algorithm 2 also thresholds range derivatives, pairs edges, checks width \(0.5\) to \(1.3\,\mathrm m\), and imposes wall membership; retaining LiDAR points does not imply these stages output the door. Likewise P\(\text{\u2019}\)s mean room-dimension error \(201.5\,\mathrm{mm}\) in Table 2 (lines 527-560) cannot be compared directly to the \(150\,\mathrm{mm}\) gate as a wall-offset bound, because dimension error, wall thickness correction, and point-to-wall distance differ. A conditional full-field audit is only robust if it is genuinely complete for visible doors under the stated sensor/noise model, and the objective must include scan/actuation cost and missed-door delay. Otherwise the generic Q vocabulary adds no new result.

Caveat to #9: “occasional audits” alone do not yield worst-case door discovery. A door visible for only one scan may fall between audits; even persistent visibility gives no bounded latency unless audit gaps are bounded. If a prediction-independent full-field detector is complete whenever a door remains visible for \(\tau\) consecutive scans, auditing at least once per \(\tau\)-scan window yields discovery delay at most \(\tau\) scans after first visibility, with added full-scan work about \(N^2/\tau\) per scan under P’s all-pairs implementation. This is a conditional sampling/compute tradeoff, not a competitive-ratio theorem for robot navigation. Alternatively a sound online wall-error certificate allows no audit on certified scans, but P provides no such certificate; matching residuals inside the gate cannot certify omitted walls.

Primary-source cross-check of Ada\(\text{\u2019}\)s analogous prior: Xu et al., Deep GrabCut for Object Selection, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.00243, abstract and pp. 1-2, explicitly criticizes hard predicted bounding-box crops because they omit object/context and replaces the box with a soft distance-map prior while retaining the whole image. This means replacing P\(\text{\u2019}\)s hard gate by a soft spatial prior is also a known general design pattern. A publication-worthy contribution would need the P-specific geometry/topology interface, a proved sensing/search objective, and comparative experiments; the elementary distance lemma and generic soft gating alone are insufficient.

Best account from my side: I change the question from “can Q give P a door-detector competitive ratio?” to “can room-wall error be certified or periodically audited so P’s geometric prior saves work without censoring visible doors?” Q already warns that arbitrary fallbacks and component triples do not transfer automatically (Q.tex lines 1016, 1023-1026, 1116-1119), and its PGM case illustrates certified local search as an existing pattern (lines 1143-1148). P supplies the concrete failure interface: the \(0.15\,\mathrm m\) wall gate, all-pairs candidate generation and later wall test (P.tex lines 352-385), no revision of accepted wrong rooms (lines 615-630), and simplified evaluations with topology correct only in tested cases (lines 481-560). Research contribution would require (i) a sound bound on missing-wall/point error or an explicit audit schedule, (ii) a candidate generator with proved completeness under visibility/noise and width margins, (iii) an objective such as missed-door delay plus compute/robot-motion cost with a prediction-free comparator, and (iv) controlled perturbation experiments including omitted walls and nonrectangular rooms. The elementary \(b+\epsilon\) gate lemma alone is insufficient and existing soft-prior and graph-exploration work limit novelty. I view this as a credible scoped project, not yet a proven publishable result.

Best account so far: replace the abstract question “apply Q consistency/robustness to P” by “under what geometric margins and visibility/audit assumptions can P’s room-conditioned search retain every visible door, and what compute/detection-delay tradeoff results?” Q (lines 257-343, 1023-1110) supplies the discipline of declaring prediction error, system objective, comparator, and edge sensitivity, not a ready-made door theorem. P (lines 195-205, 352-429, 603-633) supplies the specific hard gate, downstream tests, asynchronous activation, and fixed-wrong-model failure. Negative result: without revision or a complete prediction-independent audit, a persistently omitted wall permits infinite missed-door latency despite finite full-field discovery. Positive first step: \(\operatorname{dist}(p,\hat W)\leq b+\epsilon\) under one-sided wall error \(\epsilon\) and point noise \(b\), so widening the gate retains relevant points if \(\delta\geq b+\epsilon\); further edge/width/wall margins and sensor visibility are needed for recall. Ada\(\text{\u2019}\)s #12 correctly notes bounded audit gaps and persistent visibility are necessary for finite discovery delay. Publication potential is conditional and moderate: formalize a nontrivial complete baseline and a certified/adaptive gate, then demonstrate a measurable compute-versus-recall/delay frontier on wrong-room, occluded, nonrectangular, and revision cases. Generic LAA reframing or soft gating alone is too familiar (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05422 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.00243). Unresolved: whether P’s raw-scan/full-field detector can be complete under realistic noise, whether an online wall-error certificate is attainable without seeing excluded evidence, and whether such a result improves relevant prior work.

Cross-check of Ada #18 against P Algorithm 2 (lines 352-389) and its fixed-model limitation (lines 613-630): agreed. A sparse audit schedule only bounds discovery delay under persistent visibility spanning an audit; transient one-scan doors require auditing that scan or a retained raw-data replay with its own completeness/storage assumptions. Thus the useful theorem target is conditional: wall-error margins certify candidate retention on gated scans; bounded-gap complete audits cover uncertified scans under a stated visibility window. Q\(\text{\u2019}\)s cascade/error-propagation conditions (lines 1069-1110) explain why neither local statement automatically yields system-level navigation guarantees. The remaining scientific risk is whether such assumptions and the resulting work-delay frontier are both realistic and stronger than known soft-prior/exploration methods.
